title: Coleman Hawkins's refusal to look back, and his love of argument
summary: Hawkins insisted he never played slap-tongue solos, even when Barefield brought a Henderson record. Barefield describes him as loving musical arguments and being a fine reader, writer and pianist.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: And the funny thing about it, Hawkins never liked to look back at things, you know. So we used to do an arrangement on -- I was only playing clarinet then, by the way, because we had Hawk and myself and I forget who was playing trumpet at that time. So we were doing -- did the St. Louis Blues. And in rehearsal Hawk said, well, we'll play it with an old ragtime feeling, a corney feeling, and everybody take a ragtime solo, you know. And when they got to his solo he just went on and played, you know. So I said, well, Hawk, why don't you play one of them oldtime Fletcher Henderson slap-tone solos that you used to play. "I never played like that. I never played anything like that." I said, okay, I'll bring you a record tomorrow. And I brought Dick DoGlyde up where he was slap-timing, you know. And he said, "no, man, that wasn't me. I don't want to hear that, you know.
He was a marvelous guy. I liked Hawk.
He liked to argue, didn't he?
He liked to argue for the say, you know.
Well, musically he liked to agitate a little bit, you know. He loved a good jam session and a good musical argument, you know. Where -- that was right in his --
Well, I remember once I was in his company and he was having an argument with somebody about the merits of Horowitz and Reubenstein and he was a Reubenstein man.

Yeah, he loved all of that. Anything musical, you know, he loved to get into that, playing in different keys, you know. He was very up on his instrument and his music, you know. And he was a good reader, he was a writer, he was a pianist. And he was really -- he wasn't underrated at all. He was the daddy. And I always recognized that. And all of the guys like Ben Webster and these guys Hawk loved like Don Byas and Ben Webster, they were all good friends. But they had their differences, you know.
